lead.headline: The DMK backs the Centre's delimitation bill and attacks the Congress, as the INDIA bloc meets to plan its fight in the special session
lead.short: A meeting of DMK MPs chaired by M.K. Stalin on Saturday backed the new constitutional amendment on delimitation, as long as Tamil Nadu keeps its 7.18% share of Lok Sabha seats, and accused the Congress of a "treacherous act". In Delhi, INDIA bloc floor leaders met at Mallikarjun Kharge's home to agree a joint strategy before the special session.

why.text: How seats are shared between states after the freeze ends decides the political weight of the south for decades.

more: The DMK demanded that each state's share, fixed on the 1971 Census, stay frozen for another 25 years, and told the Congress, its former ally, to stop lecturing it on principles. The revised bill extends the population freeze to 2051 and narrows Parliament's discretion on delimitation. A similar attempt was defeated in the Lok Sabha in April.

Rahul Gandhi, the TMC's Abhishek Banerjee, Kapil Sibal and leaders of the RJD, CPI, IUML and RSP joined the opposition meeting; the DMK, AAP and BJD were invited but stayed away. "If this Bill is passed, the number of Lok Sabha seats could increase to around 850," Sibal said. "We are ready for women's reservation. They can implement it immediately within the existing 543 seats."

update.new: The DMK backs the bill; the opposition meets.
update.front: The DMK, a BJP rival, has now come out for the bill.

seconds.headline: An Israeli strike on a clearly marked Doctors Without Borders clinic in Gaza City kills two of its watchmen
seconds.short: Two Doctors Without Borders staff, both watchmen, were killed in an Israeli strike on its clinic in Gaza City on Friday night, the charity said, calling it a "direct hit". MSF said the premises were clearly marked with its logos and their location was known to the Israeli military. Its toll of staff killed in Gaza is now 17.

why.text: Attacks on aid workers keep rising in Gaza, where Israel has blocked MSF's international staff since January.

more: "We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues," MSF said. The Israeli military claimed, without providing evidence, that the two were members of Hamas. The World Health Organization's chief, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, called the attack "outrageous and unacceptable". "Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked," he wrote.

Israel's forces have killed more than 1,700 health workers in Gaza since October 2023. In January, MSF said Israel had blocked its supplies and denied entry to all its international staff since the start of the year. Aid groups say Israeli claims linking them to Hamas have helped normalise attacks on humanitarian workers.

update.new: A strike kills two MSF staff.
update.front: A strike on a marked medical clinic, killing aid workers, is news in itself.

seconds.headline: A US aircraft disables a ship leaving Iran in the Gulf of Oman, and Kuwait summons Iran's ambassador over the Italians' deaths
seconds.short: A US aircraft fired "precision munitions" into the stern of the Palau-flagged Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman on Friday, disabling it, after it left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas in breach of the US blockade, Central Command said. The civilian crew was unharmed. Kuwait summoned Iran's ambassador over Thursday's strike that killed two Italian technicians.

why.text: Both sides are pressing harder at sea and on Gulf soil, and the UN warns renewed war would hit the region and beyond.

more: The blockade of Iranian ports, launched in mid-July after an agreement with Tehran collapsed, has now disabled six ships and redirected 158 others, CENTCOM says. The war began in February when the US and Israel struck Iran, which responded by imposing its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz. CENTCOM said it "continues to strictly enforce" the blockade.

Kuwait's deputy foreign minister, Hamad Al-Mashaan, condemned "continued Iranian attacks" and said Kuwait reserved its right to self-defence. UN Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the strike and urged "all parties to exercise restraint", his spokesman said. "Renewed hostilities would have devastating consequences for the region and beyond."

update.new: The US disables a ship; Kuwait summons Iran's envoy.
update.front: The US has now fired on a ship breaking its blockade.

seconds.headline: The food regulator finds coliform bacteria in a second Bisleri sample, from a batch made in West Bengal in July
seconds.short: India's food regulator, the FSSAI, has found a second Bisleri water sample unsafe, this time because of coliform bacteria, a regulatory document shows. In a 12 August notice, it told the company to stop selling the affected batch, made in July, and a confirmation test still found it unsafe. Bisleri says it recalled the batch, PB201.

why.text: It is the second failed sample in days for India's best-known bottled water, as the regulator tests every brand.

more: Bisleri said on Saturday that the batch came from its plant at Telipara in West Bengal's Jalpaiguri district, and that the FSSAI barred its sale on 12 August. "The primary and referral laboratories reported the presence of coliform bacteria in the regulatory sample," the company said.

It said it had samples from the same batch tested at two independent laboratories recognised by the FSSAI, and both found them within the standard for coliform bacteria and all other food safety rules. The first failed sample, reported last week, had too much bromate, and a retest found polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons. The FSSAI has since begun testing samples from every bottled water brand.

facts.Bisleri: two private labs found it safe

update.new: A second sample fails, for bacteria.
update.front: A second failed test, now for bacteria, widens the case against India's biggest water brand.

stories.headline: Tamil Nadu police arrest TVK MLA Arul Vignesh over a woman IAS officer's harassment complaint, after the High Court stepped in
stories.short: Tamil Nadu police on Friday arrested C. Arul Vignesh, MLA from the ruling Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam, over a harassment complaint by a woman IAS officer, four days after she went to the police and after the Madras High Court placed the inquiry under senior officers. He was arrested at his home in Kallakurichi. He denies wrongdoing.

why.text: It tests whether the ruling TVK will let police act against one of its own legislators.

more: Police said the officer complained on 23 November and the Kallakurichi All Women Police Station registered a case that day, a Monday, not on Tuesday as the government told the High Court. After the court's 24 November order, Tiruppur superintendent Shristi Singh took over the case under Inspector General N. Kamini.

Vignesh had called the allegations politically motivated. The court acted on a petition by advocate R. Thrishuli seeking an FIR and a fair investigation. A separate workplace harassment inquiry is also under way, and police say the investigation continues. Police had been posted around his home and office since the case was registered.

stories.headline: Spain votes on Sunday with Feijóo's conservatives narrowly ahead, and Sánchez says he "cannot imagine us losing"
stories.short: Spain's party leaders held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's general election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls. "I cannot imagine us losing," he said, accusing his conservative rival, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, of planning a coalition with the far right. Feijóo's People's Party is narrowly ahead in the polls.

why.text: A Sánchez defeat would take one of Europe's few left-wing governments out of power, with France voting five months later.

more: Feijóo promised a new era of "truth, decency and good governance" and accused Sánchez of dodging questions on corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt. "This time, yes, we're going to do it," he said, three years after winning the most seats but failing to form a government.

If he does govern, it will be with the support of Vox, the anti-immigration party led by Santiago Abascal, which held its final rally in a Valencia bull-ring. Almost 39 million people can vote, and no polls have been published since Monday under Spanish electoral law. Most suggest a close finish.

stories.headline: Taiwan votes for 11,000 local posts, with the Taipei race between Chiang Wan-an and Puma Shen the one Beijing is watching
stories.short: Taiwan voted on Saturday for mayors, councillors and other local leaders in its "nine-in-one" elections, with about 11,000 posts at stake across 22 cities and counties. Polls closed at 13:30 IST, with results expected this evening. The key race is in Taipei, where Kuomintang mayor Chiang Wan-an faces the ruling DPP's Puma Shen.

why.text: A DPP win in the opposition's Taipei heartland would embarrass Beijing, which has branded Shen a separatist.

more: Shen, an academic-turned-lawmaker and expert on China's information warfare, is wanted by Chinese police for "separatism". He began as the underdog but drew huge crowds; an online rally drew more than 500,000 viewers on YouTube. A Shen win would be "quite shameful" for Beijing, said Austin Wang of the University of Nevada.

The vote will not directly change Taiwan's China policy, and campaigns focused on transport, childcare and the environment. Other key races are in New Taipei City and Kaohsiung. Taiwan's defence ministry counted about 33 sorties by Chinese warplanes towards the island between Friday and Saturday, including bombers and fighter jets.

stories.headline: The RBI eases banks' daily cash reserve rule back to 90% from 99% as liquidity slips into deficit
stories.short: The Reserve Bank of India has rolled back its tighter daily cash reserve ratio rule, letting banks keep a minimum of 90% of the required CRR each day instead of 99%, from 1 December, as banking liquidity has slipped into deficit. The overall CRR stays at 3%. The deficit was ₹47,641 crore on 26 November.

why.text: Tight cash in the banks raises short-term borrowing costs, which could weigh on growth if it lasts.

more: Liquidity swung from a surplus of nearly ₹11 trillion on 13 September to a deficit of ₹12,825 crore on 21 November, the first since June. The RBI had raised the daily requirement in October to soak up money from the FCNR-B deposit scheme, which drew $133 billion. Its currency interventions and other operations have since drained cash.

"Once core liquidity starts coming down to around ₹4 trillion levels, you will be in a persistent system liquidity deficit situation," said Gaura Sengupta of IDFC FIRST Bank. Government spending could push liquidity briefly into surplus in December, but she expects a persistent deficit in the fourth quarter.

stories.headline: OpenAI countersues Apple, accusing it of stealing trade secrets about its devices and leaning on suppliers
stories.short: OpenAI sued Apple on Friday in federal court in northern California, accusing it of stealing trade secrets and discouraging hardware suppliers from working on OpenAI's future devices. It said Apple gained confidential information by rehiring a former employee who spent six months at OpenAI, with access to a new device and its hardware roadmap. Apple denies it.

why.text: The two are now fighting over who builds the AI gadget that could replace the phone.

more: "Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place," OpenAI said. It said its AI devices threaten to "outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf", and that Apple's employment practices were designed to "trap" staff. Apple called the claims "a transparent attempt to distract".

Apple sued OpenAI in July, with former employees Tang Tan and Chang Liu, alleging misappropriation of its trade secrets. Tan, a 24-year Apple veteran who led iPhone and Apple Watch product design, co-founded io Products, which OpenAI bought in 2025. OpenAI says Apple's case rests on unauthorised monitoring of Liu's personal messages.

facts.claim: trade secrets and pressure on suppliers
